Consulting Mindset

About

I work at the intersection of research and strategy — translating complex market data into decision-ready intelligence that drives business action. My work spans competitive benchmarking, market sizing, and executive reporting, always anchored in the question: what does this mean for the business?

With coverage across ICT, Chemicals, Automotive, Industrial, and Consumer sectors, I bring a structured analytical lens to every engagement. Frameworks like SWOT, PESTLE, and Porter's Five Forces are tools for genuine strategic thinking — helping stakeholders understand competitive dynamics, regulatory environments, and the market forces that shape outcomes.

My research exposure includes focused work on Japan's industrial and automotive manufacturing landscape, providing a nuanced view of how regional market structures diverge from Western frameworks. Combined with strong stakeholder collaboration skills, this enables me to bridge research depth with clear business narrative.

Superstore Sales Performance — KPI cards, category & sub-category breakdown, order priority, monthly trends & regional map
Power BI Dashboard

Superstore — Sales Performance

Objective

Provide leadership with a real-time view of sales health, profitability, and regional distribution to support commercial decision-making.

What It Analyzes

Total sales ($2.30M, ↑4.10% vs last month), profit ($286.40K, ↑3.07%), quantity (37.87K, ↑4.94%), and average discount ($0.16). Breaks down sales by category (Technology $83.62K, Furniture $74.20K, Office Supplies $71.90K), profit by sub-category (Phones $45K, Paper $34K, Tables -$18K), order priority split (Medium 57.2%, High 30.56%), and monthly sales & profit trends with geographic distribution across global regions.

Insight HighlightTechnology leads category sales while Tables show negative profit (-$18K) — signalling a pricing or cost issue that warrants immediate review. Q4 peaks in monthly trends support forward resource planning.
Business Value

Enables executives to identify underperforming sub-categories, monitor month-on-month momentum, and allocate resources to high-growth regions — all from a single dashboard view.

Superstore — Product & Shipping

Objective

Analyze how product categories and shipping efficiency interact to affect profitability, enabling operations teams to optimize fulfillment strategies.

What It Analyzes

Sales by product category (Office Supplies 348,996 | Phones 330,007 | Tables 206,966), profit by category (Technology $145.46K, Office Supplies $122.49K, Furniture $18.45K), profit & avg shipping cost across delivery day ranges, order volume vs. shipping efficiency by delivery days, profit by delivery bucket (5–7 days $112K, 3–4 days $98K, 0–2 days $76K), and sub-category scatter of shipping cost vs profit vs quantity.

Insight HighlightOrders delivered in 5–7 days generate the highest profit ($112K) vs 0–2 day deliveries ($76K) — revealing a clear cost-speed trade-off that warrants operational review. Copiers and Phones lead profitability in the sub-category scatter.
Business Value

Helps operations and commercial teams identify optimal delivery windows and high-margin product-shipping combinations to improve contribution margins.

Learning in Practice

Market Sizing — What I'm Learning

Market sizing is a skill I've been actively building. Here's how I've been practising it — using the Packaged Drinking Water market as a simple example to understand the core approach.

What is Market Sizing?

At its core, market sizing is answering: "How big is this market?" — not with a guess, but with a structured, logical estimate built from real data.

In my work in market research, I've seen market sizing referenced constantly — in client reports, feasibility studies, and competitive analysis. I decided to actually learn the basic methods so I can contribute more meaningfully to these deliverables.

I'm still in the early stages — but the approach I've practised is: start with a real market, use free official data, apply a simple method, and sanity-check the result.

Practice Market

I chose Global Packaged Drinking Water because it's a straightforward consumer market — easy to understand, with clear data available from WHO, FAO, and World Bank.

Two Methods I Practised
Top-Down — Start from the big picture

Take a large known number (world GDP or total beverage market) and narrow it down using percentage estimates at each level until you reach your product.

World GDP → F&B Sector (4.2%)
→ Beverages → Packaged Water
≈ $315 Bn estimate
Bottom-Up — Build from individual units

Estimate who buys the product, how much they buy, and at what price — then multiply up to get the total market size. More granular and defensible.

Population × % without tap water (WHO)
× Litres/year × Price per litre
≈ $256–326 Bn range

What I Learned

The core formula is simple

Forecast Year = Base Year × (1 + Growth Rate)^n. Once I understood this, building the table in Excel was straightforward — I just needed reliable numbers to plug in.

Data sourcing is half the work

I used WHO drinking water reports, World Bank GDP data, and UN Comtrade for trade volumes. Finding the right free data source was more challenging than the calculation itself.

Cross-checking gives confidence

Running both top-down and bottom-up methods and comparing results (I got ~$315Bn vs ~$320Bn) showed me that the estimate was directionally right — even if not perfectly precise.

What I want to improve

I'm working on getting better at setting growth rate assumptions with more rigour, and understanding regional splits. This is an area I'm actively building on.
